talks.title: Cyber Leadership: Resilience, Risk and Strategic Decision-Making
talks.teaser: Senior security leaders explain board communication, resilience measurement, and aligning cyber strategy with business objectives.
talks.summary:
The session opens with security leaders from transport, aviation, banking, and healthcare describing how the CISO role has widened: faster exploitation cycles, heavier regulation, and stronger expectations to evidence controls while influencing budgets and the board. Panelists argue boards care about risk, cost, and revenue more than technical detail, so effective updates use business language, residual risk framing, customer impact, and plain board papers while inviting feedback and bringing plans—not just worries.

On resilience, speakers treat it as operating through disruption, not only recovery. Themes include rapid detection, supply chain exposure, truly offline backups, limiting blast radius, and planning for scenarios where IT may be unavailable. They tie crown jewels to customer-critical services, stress people-and-process exercises beyond pure security drills, and test backup and recovery assumptions regularly.

For strategy, they urge linking cyber plans to business objectives, embedding secure foundations in digital programs, using regulation such as DORA as a baseline, and staying close to operations—not working in a silo. Closing advice covers simplifying messages for executives, shared accountability across the enterprise, developing teams, watching extended supply chains, and balancing AI innovation with patching and hygiene fundamentals. Audience questions touch on AI control trade-offs, securing low-budget nonprofits, media-driven targeting, and influencing upward from earlier-career roles through risk literacy and collaboration.

talks.title: How do we break the cycle of Teenage Cybercrime?
talks.teaser: A journalist traces adolescent hacking crews from game outages to major breaches and what might interrupt the cycle.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with the 2020 Vastaamo psychotherapy breach in Finland, where tens of thousands of patients received personalized extortion emails threatening publication of therapy notes. The speaker describes how poorly secured central records enabled a quick theft, escalating pressure through partial leaks, and how a later mistake helped identify the attacker, who was eventually arrested abroad and convicted.

The core thread is the pathway from teenage online delinquency to headline-grabbing crime. Examples include the 2014 Lizard Squad Christmas disruptions of gaming networks, Allison Nixon’s “noob persistent threat” framing, and how groups such as LulzSec shifted hacking culture toward chaos and publicity. More recent cases—Lapsus$, Scattered Spider, and affiliations with ransomware-as-a-service operations—show teens pairing social engineering with established criminal infrastructure, Bitcoin, and compulsive reoffending despite arrests.

Practitioners should expect disproportionate harm from actors who crave attention, troll investigators, and partner with mature criminal economies. The closing argument is that blaming only nation-states obscures a recurring pipeline of adolescent offenders, leaving victims, companies, and the young offenders themselves caught in a cycle that law enforcement and the security industry have repeatedly failed to interrupt.

talks.title: Safeguarding Critical Infrastructure from the Cyber Threats of Today
talks.teaser: Safeguarding Critical Infrastructure from the Cyber Threats of Today.

talks.title: Building A Winning Cybersecurity Strategy in the Era of AI
talks.teaser: Reframes AI-era security strategy around trust, visibility and correctness, with practical shifts for teams adopting agents.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that AI is changing the foundations security strategies rest on, rather than simply being a tool that can do security. The speaker names three pillars now under strain: trust, visibility and correctness. Deepfakes and synthetic images make identities and content hard to verify, while growing data volumes make a single source of truth harder to reach. Examples such as an agent deleting a company's database in 9 seconds and a chatbot agreeing to sell a car for a dollar showed automated decisions based on statistical guesses rather than reality.

To rebuild those pillars, the speaker proposed four shifts. Verification should replace trust, meaning constant checks of identity, intent and behaviour rather than a single login. Orchestration should replace buying more tools, so products share data and decisions, with humans kept in the loop. Architecture should replace policy documents, so required restrictions are built into systems rather than left to teams to follow. Reliable outcomes should replace AI adoption for its own sake, judged by accuracy, reliability and the impact of decisions.

In the Q&A, the speaker said legacy tools should be judged by what they deliver, and that foundational visibility and detections remain valid. AI should be applied narrowly to help analysts work faster.

talks.title: When Identity becomes the Attack Path
talks.teaser: Surveys current adversaries and shows how stolen identities let attackers move quickly through an organization.
talks.summary:
The talk surveys the threat landscape, from nation-state groups and activists to a fast-growing criminal ecosystem. Its core message is that attackers often just log in with valid credentials. Breakout time, the gap before an intruder starts moving laterally, shows the pace: 48 minutes for the fastest case in 2025, an average of 29 minutes last year, and 27 seconds in the quickest case, which involved stolen credentials.

Recent examples show how this works. A package library on PyPI was taken over after an attacker injected code through an open pull request and stole a GitHub token, so installers received an information stealer targeting cloud and crypto-wallet credentials. Fake Claude download pages for Windows and macOS delivered malicious tools. In a voice phishing case, a group posing as the IT help desk pushed authentication requests, then used remote-assistance software for full access. China was also described as weaponising public patches quickly.

The speaker's advice centres on identity: check context such as user risk, device and request legitimacy rather than relying on MFA alone, adopt phishing-resistant authentication, use risk-based access, and remove standing privileges. Teams also need full visibility across cloud and SaaS environments, smarter patch prioritisation, and tooling that can handle large incident volumes. Security should be part of AI adoption from the start.

talks.title: The State of Cybersecurity 2026
talks.teaser: Coverage of The State of Cybersecurity 2026 from the conference program.

talks.title: ZDC25: Ronan Murphy, Founder Smarttech247 - How AI Is Shaping Our Future (Closing Comments)
talks.teaser: Surveys the AI revolution and argues that data protection and AI risk management will shape security's future.
talks.summary:
This closing talk frames AI as the start of a fifth industrial revolution, comparing it with earlier shifts from steam, electricity and computing. It describes office work being reshaped by AI assistants, and a fast-moving competition in which China's DeepSeek R1 and Alibaba's QwQ 32B were presented as signs that the field is changing quickly. The speaker also recalls the Paris AI summit, where the United States declined to sign a declaration on sustainable AI, and contrasts that approach with the EU AI Act.

The core argument is that data is the layer organisations keep responsible for even as they outsource infrastructure to cloud and software services, and that it is the thing attackers want most. A short video showed a deepfake of a young person whose photos are used to build a fake identity, scam relatives by voice and damage her credit. From this, the speaker argues for regulation at the application layer rather than at research level, and describes data detect and respond as a way for a security operations centre to classify data and enforce policy in real time.

Looking ahead, the talk predicts three developments: multimodal retrieval augmented generation that reduces outdated answers, agentic AI that plans and acts with human oversight, and robotics in manufacturing and logistics. The closing takeaway is that AI risk management is likely to become a large sector over the next fifteen years, and that whether AI is good or bad depends on how it is implemented.

talks.title: ZDC25: Roel Schouten, Trivium Packaging
talks.teaser: Argues that colleagues should be treated as allies rather than weakest links, and shows how one manufacturer applies that idea.
talks.summary:
In this session, Roel Schouten, information security lead at Trivium Packaging, a metal packaging manufacturer, argues that colleagues should be treated as allies rather than weak links. The speaker opens with a bed bug story: people hear a warning, forget it, and security awareness messages suffer the same fate. Cited research found that most users who took risky actions knew they were doing so, usually for convenience.

After a 2021 ransomware attack caused about three months of downtime, the security team set out to stop being seen as the department of no. Staff are encouraged to speak with people on the production floor. Where possible, controls are enforced technically instead of requested from users: single sign-on, access only from managed devices, automatic browser updates and web filtering, with password changes required only after a risky event. The speaker also calls several common tips outdated, including avoiding public Wi-Fi, always using a VPN and banning private use of company devices.

Staff receive just three messages: store and share with care, think before you click, and see it, report it, stop it. For phishing, strict filters quarantine suspicious mail, and a person checks each message before it is released. Users who report suspicious emails get feedback, and the talk closes with the CEO admitting in a company town hall that he had clicked a phishing email and urging everyone to report such mail.

talks.title: ZDC25: Mark Woods, Splunk - Walking the Tightrope: Navigating Risk, Impact and Change
talks.teaser: ZDC25: Mark Woods, Splunk - Walking the Tightrope: Navigating Risk, Impact and Change.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Mark Woods, Chief Technical Adviser from Splunk, explores the challenges of defining and measuring resilience across complex organizational systems. Reflecting on his past experience leading an engineering team through a major core system upgrade, Woods highlights the common dilemma of delivering projects on time and within tolerance while still lacking a clear understanding of actual service resilience. The presentation focuses on bridging the gap between low-level technical operations and high-level business leadership by grounding resilience in service context, capacity, and impact.

### Key Topics
- **Defining Resilience**: Resilience cannot be treated as a simple tick-box exercise or merely surviving a crisis. Using a Formula 1 analogy, Woods explains that resilience is not just about passing pre-race inspections or crossing the finish line, but how well a system performs and endures throughout an entire dynamic operating environment. Broadly, resilience comprises both recovery (the ability to respond when something happens) and absorption (the capacity to absorb changes or disruptions without needing an active operational response).
- **Bridging 'Board to Keyboard'**: Technical teams typically evaluate significance and health bottom-up from component-level or system-level metrics, while leadership and boards focus on business opportunities, change capacity, and top-level risk profiles. Woods argues for aligning these viewpoints through shared operational health and service context rather than relying on raw incident counts.
- **Ambidextrous Delivery and Agility**: Organizations must balance risk mitigation (building robustness, absorption, and recovery) with opportunity exploitation (moving quickly, launching new features, and driving innovation). Over-indexing on pure resilience limits change, while moving fast without resilience creates excessive failure and maintenance toil.
- **The Insight Ladder and Shared Context**: Operational teams and leadership often interpret data differently depending on whether they are focusing on day-to-day execution or macro-level business challenges. Woods notes that there is "no one ring to rule them all" in terms of tooling or metrics; instead, alignment comes from shared context around critical services and understanding end-user impact.

### Technical Details & Operational Measurement
- **Right Capacity vs. Total Visibility**: Woods cautions against the trap of chasing end-to-end, full-fidelity visibility across all possible component interactions, noting that it assumes infinite budgets and team capacity. Instead, organizations must identify the right capacity tailored to prioritized critical services.
- **Service Context & Impact**: Rather than viewing resilience strictly within functional silos (e.g., pure network, compute, or infrastructure levels), resilience must be measured at the service and product level. Risk and performance metrics should reflect the direct impact on internal and external end users rather than abstract system counts.
- **Security's Role**: Security teams possess a unique advantage because their workflows inherently rely on data, detections, context, and response. By extending this contextual data approach to services and business products, security can actively enable broader organizational resilience.

### Takeaways
- Resilience requires balancing the right capacity for absorption and recovery against the organization's appetite for change and agility.
- Raw operational counts (e.g., reducing an arbitrary metric from 1,000 to 900) do not automatically translate to increased resilience unless tied to service impact.
- Measuring operational resilience around prioritized critical services provides a common language between technical operators and executive leadership.

talks.title: ZDC25: Shaping the Future - Leadership Strategies for Cybersecurity and Risk Management
talks.teaser: Panelists outline cyber alignment, shadow AI, regulation, and resilience drills across aviation, energy, insurance, and pharma.
talks.summary:
A moderated panel explores how chief information security officer roles have shifted as cyber programs must support the full business value chain. Participants from aviation cargo, renewable-energy drone operations, general insurance, and rare-disease therapeutics describe aligning cyber risk with frameworks they already use for safety, finance, and operations rather than treating security as a bolt-on.

Discussion covers digital operational resilience regulation in financial services, venture-capital board expectations, and rising breach costs in a more complex threat landscape. Panelists outline shadow artificial intelligence among employees, deliberate product-model choices, and sudden AI features embedded in existing vendor tools that expand subprocessors. They stress leadership-level policy, data-handling discipline, and supply-chain visibility when tools clash or enable features without notice.

Resilience themes include medical and manufacturing continuity, contract-manufacturer downstream impact, inclusive incident exercises that build executive muscle memory, and using real weather and claims events as practice incidents. Closing reflections favor crisis-driven investment, regular executive simulations, phishing campaigns paired with open reporting culture, and plain-language communication that security is everyone’s responsibility.

talks.title: ZDC25: Eoin McGrath, ThreatLocker
talks.teaser: Walks through anonymized ransomware cases, from initial access to encryption, and the controls that could have stopped them.
talks.summary:
The talk follows a typical ransomware attack in stages: initial access, reconnaissance using tools already on the network, locating backups and insurance details, delivering a payload, and encryption, sometimes done remotely over network shares. Common entry points include exposed remote desktop, fake remote access tools, reverse shells and unpatched VPNs.

The presenter describes two anonymized cases. A US manufacturer with about 400 staff opened a Word document link that installed a remote access tool. Attackers scanned the network with an in-memory tool, brute forced accounts with net use, which blended into clock-skew login noise, and reached a domain controller over RDP. They pushed ransomware through a Group Policy object and a PowerShell script, after taking a sample of files for extortion. In the second case, a global healthcare organization was breached through an unpatched VPN device. Attackers used Cobalt Strike to find vulnerable endpoints, then used EternalBlue on a domain server to push encryption out.

The advice centres on blocking untrusted software, allowlisting known applications, removing unneeded remote access tools, stopping PowerShell from reaching the internet, restricting RDP to a dynamic list of allowed addresses, and patching network hardware. A demo showed a known reverse shell being blocked while an AI-generated one with the same function ran because it was unknown. The main point is to stop unauthorized software and limit what approved software can do.

talks.title: Panel Discussion - Your Data is Gone. How Did You Get Here? Building Better Cyber Resilience
talks.teaser: Panelists discuss recovering from data loss, covering backups, incident response plans, staff readiness and MFA limits.
talks.summary:
The panel brings together an insurance broker, a healthcare research CIO and a security vendor representative to discuss how organisations recover when their data is lost. They argue that resilience starts from the assumption that a breach has already happened, and that the gap between written plans and what people actually do under pressure is where many responses fail. Recovery also depends on knowing which systems hold which data, and that information is rarely documented in advance.

The speakers describe practical measures: classifying data and assessing its value, keeping backups offline or immutable and confirming they can actually be restored, locking down privileged access and service accounts, enabling auditing, and maintaining asset inventories. They note that multi-factor authentication helps but is not a complete answer, since attackers now trick users into approving prompts or intercepting codes. Drills and tabletop exercises are recommended, though one speaker warns that tabletops carry optimism bias and that real restores take longer because of missed dependencies. Incident response plans should be flexible, name the decision-makers, and be practised.

On the human side, the panel points to stress on recovery teams, low morale when the wider organisation does not understand what responders are going through, and the need for accurate risk profiles that treat cyber events with the same seriousness as physical safety hazards. The closing advice is to admit the problem early, rehearse recovery for real rather than only on paper, and keep asset records current as the organisation changes.

talks.title: ZDC23: Edward Skraba, Smarttech247 - How They Got Hacked?
talks.teaser: Four red-team case studies show how supposedly secured organizations still fall to OSINT, custom exploits, and weak controls.
talks.summary:
The presenter opens by arguing that stronger tooling and threat intelligence have not stopped intrusions, and outlines an attack infrastructure built for distributed operations, disposable proxies, and defense evasion—including switchblade-style hidden command channels. He structures engagements as reconnaissance, initial access, persistence, discovery, escalation, and post-exploitation, always with detection in mind.

Four examples follow. An international education institute assessment starting from only a name yields domain admin via leaked credentials, a custom exploit for an application without public signatures, a stealth web shell, and cleartext admin passwords in files. A European university engagement uses thousands of leaked passwords, kiosk-style sandbox escape without malware, and highlights vendor trust misplaced on sandbox boundaries. Phishing cases bypass anti-phishing by delivering images directly to the mail server and abuse SPF configurations that trust provider IP ranges. A web application test against a software house chains cross-site scripting into development and hosting environments, compromises all client apps, and could poison future releases. He also notes physical ingress at a Polish electronics facility and demonstrates radio or NFC cloning with a handheld device.

Takeaways stress asset discovery for unknown assets, data classification for cleartext secrets, EDR/XDR over signature-only AV, MFA and password hygiene, threat modeling and validating third-party security claims, zero-trust between internal zones, and layered controls because impact lands at the end—not only in the middle.

talks.title: Panel Discussion - Connecting the Dots: How to Build Effective Security Programs
talks.teaser: A panel explores board buy-in, global programs, and people-centered controls for lasting organizational security.
talks.summary:
Leaders from large enterprises discuss how security programs stay effective when daily incidents pull attention away from long-term goals. They frame constant operational noise as swarms of distraction and argue that Eisenhower-style prioritization, a clear target state, and repeated training give teams shared language from the floor to the boardroom.

The conversation moves through flexible, end-to-end planning across regions, compliance and access governance at scale, and the limits of frameworks when asset inventory and skills lag behind technology. Panelists stress people-process-technology balance, risk registers that drive spending, and honest board communication using both simple risk narratives and metric-heavy backups. Examples from public breaches and newspaper headlines illustrate how executives grasp progress charts and scenario questions even when they reject jargon.

Closing themes include phishing measurement and AI voice impersonation on phone channels, mandatory identity checks on calls, resistance to incident drills, shelf-ware and half-finished deployments, and multi-year simplification in complex environments. The takeaway is that effective programs are continuous repetition: educate, measure, show progress to leadership, and align every control to business risk rather than checkbox compliance alone.

talks.title: ZDC23: Christopher McMahon, NCIS - Cybersecurity
talks.teaser: ZDC23: Christopher McMahon, NCIS - Cybersecurity.

talks.title: ZDC23: Dietmar Bettio, Aryzta - Being the Second Slowest Gazelle
talks.teaser: Argues that security is a people business built on asset transparency, strategy and feedback, not on buying tools.
talks.summary:
Dietmar Bettio opens with a food-industry analogy: his company sells bread to businesses, and a lion-and-gazelle picture of cyber security suggests aiming to be just fast enough to stay safe. He challenges that model, arguing that organisations rarely know their attacker or the slowest target, so comparing yourself to either is guesswork. He also proposes that the cost of a full day of outage, a figure insurance teams already track, is a better basis for setting security budgets than cost-cutting.

He lists gaps found at his own firm: low user awareness, staff who saw security as an IT matter, procurement that treated controls as items to negotiate, and no reliable asset inventory. He insists a CMDB is essential, since you cannot protect what you have not listed. Tools alone fail without people and processes, and he describes giving phishing-test users feedback afterwards. Controls that feel uncomfortable, he adds, get bypassed.

He closes with a short list of measures: an accurate CMDB, multi-factor authentication, a holistic strategy and stronger awareness. He reframes the analogy as being an ugly target, hard to breach and quick to handle an attack, and backs a security officer who challenges the organisation. He also urges presenting risk to boards in non-technical terms, noting that his company needed about a year to shift board perceptions.

talks.title: ZDC22: Lesley Kipling, Microsoft - Cybersecurity: it's all about the people
talks.teaser: Explores how digital empathy and culture change shape usable security, defender wellbeing, and Microsoft-scale detection operations.
talks.summary:
The session frames cybersecurity as a people and culture challenge inside a large technology company. The presenter contrasts blame-the-user cycles and heavy controls with empathy-driven design, citing desire lines and insider scenarios where staff bypass rules to deliver care, and arguing that security should work like airbags—always on but unobtrusive. Stories such as a child-friendly MRI redesign illustrate how reframing the human experience can cut fear and friction.

The middle ties the COVID-era surge in attacks—including cited figures on brute-force RDP paths into ransomware—to burnout across CISOs, analysts, and defenders drowning in noise. Microsoft’s response blends zero trust thinking with massive signal ingestion, machine learning to surface true positives, and consolidation through Defender, cloud coverage, and Sentinel-style visibility across hybrid estates. Modern principles emphasize identity as the control plane, strong authentication benefits versus low adoption, and automation so humans focus on real incidents.

Closing takeaways stress people, process, technology, and information together: hire for data skills into the SOC, embed secure defaults for developers, and measure operations with mean time to acknowledge and respond. The argument is that happier, less stressed practitioners paired with usable controls yield both productivity and stronger defense.

talks.title: Security By Design In A Digital World - 2019 Dublin
talks.teaser: Panelists discuss building security in early, protecting sensitive documents and how privacy rules shape engineering.
talks.summary:
This panel brings together people from a bank, a personalisation software company and a small Cork firm that builds data protection software to discuss security by design. The starting point is that most projects retrofit security onto systems that already exist, and that customers often hold large document repositories containing sensitive information that nobody is tracking.

The Cork company describes how it converts document text into anonymous numeric tokens and maps them into a neural network, so the original text is not kept, and it assumes its own servers could be attacked. Other examples from the discussion include infrastructure defined as code with peer review of changes, two-factor authentication and single sign-on preferred over strict password rules, and a war-game exercise that asked how hard it would be to pull data out of the network. The panel argues that insider threat means perimeter controls are not enough, and that open-source components make up sixty to ninety percent of a modern application, so they need inventories and scanning from the start of the build pipeline.

On regulation, the panel says GDPR has pushed security onto boardroom agendas because fines hit the bottom line, and compares future data compliance reports to annual financial audits. The closing advice is to know where your data sits, move security earlier into design and treat it as seriously as testing, build a culture where engineers can raise mistakes without blame, and use cloud platforms to build controls into greenfield projects.

talks.title: Ronan Murphy
talks.teaser: The keynote maps spear phishing, ransomware, breaches, GDPR, supply-chain disputes, and 5G politics to business risk and skills gaps.
talks.summary:
The session opens a Zero Day Con program in Ireland with a short industry retrospective after a prior event in Washington, framed around walking the “coalface” of security—the good, the bad, and the worst of what practitioners see in practice.

The speaker argues that adversaries have sharpened spear phishing using dark-web data and compromised email, driving invoice fraud and ransomware. He cites roughly twenty international ransomware victims his organization has engaged, describes attacks on file shares and backups, and walks through high-profile breach cases including Marriott (passport data, encryption keys stored with ciphertext, suspected state involvement and share-price impact) and British Airways (card skimming under GDPR, rapid disclosure). He connects those incidents to market reactions, uneven breach transparency, French regulatory action against large tech firms, the disputed Bloomberg Super Micro supply-chain story, and intensifying Western scrutiny of Huawei as 5G rolls out, including concerns about telecommunications kill switches during crises.

Looking ahead, he highlights a multi-million-person cybersecurity skills shortfall, weak diversity in technical roles, dual-use advances in artificial intelligence, cloud adoption where most security failures are blamed on customers, growing attack surfaces, and a regulatory environment that is already reshaping how organizations respond and report.

talks.title: ZDC17: Panel Discussion - EU GDPR: Preparing For Cyber & Data Security Obligations
talks.teaser: Panelists discuss how organisations can prepare for GDPR's 2018 obligations, from knowing their data to handling breaches.
talks.summary:
The panel looks at the EU General Data Protection Regulation as organisations prepare for its May 2018 application. The panelists note that the regulation replaces a 1995 directive that member states implemented differently, so the new rules apply directly across the bloc and aim for a more uniform regime. They also discuss why the law was needed given how much data is now collected and processed.

Turning to practical challenges, speakers argue that much of the work is preparation: knowing which personal data is held, how it is processed and what the workflows are, whether electronic or manual. One panelist says smaller firms may not need a data protection officer if they do not process large amounts of personal data, and that many security capabilities are available to them at modest cost. Others point to vague terms like "state of the art" and a large number of undefined areas, and to the children's digital age of consent, which member states can set themselves. A breach example from the ICO website, a hospital worker viewing the wrong patient record, shows how quickly scope can grow across large record sets.

Closing advice centres on getting started, treating data governance and organisational culture as central, and raising staff awareness with simple steps such as clean desk policies. The panel agrees the deadline will not move and that compliance will be an ongoing effort rather than a one-off project.

talks.title: ZDC17: Panel Discussion
talks.teaser: Panelists from industry discuss how AI can help analysts cut alert noise while keeping humans in the loop.
talks.summary:
A closing panel at the Zero Day conference brought together speakers from IBM, Johnson Controls, SmartTech and an online gambling software firm to discuss how artificial intelligence fits into cyber security. The discussion began with the scale problem facing security operations centres, where thousands of daily alerts, log analysis and phishing reports outpace the number of analysts available. One panelist described using IBM's Watson to help analysts investigate faster and to surface incidents that would otherwise go unexamined.

Panelists agreed that AI should empower analysts rather than replace them. One speaker described separating noise from real events across millions of field devices that generate billions of signals a day, and stressed that human feedback is needed so a system learns why an answer was wrong. Another described a gambling platform building predictive analytics to tell natural traffic from brute-force login attempts, where a wrong block could be very costly. Panelists also suggested AI could help with data classification for GDPR, and that sharing normalised data across an industry could reveal patterns such as match fixing.

On the threat side, the panel did not see attackers' use of AI as an immediate concern. The closing points were that AI's value lies in speed and accuracy, that its cost is small compared with the damage of a breach, and that organisations should capture data now so it can be analysed later. Speakers also noted that staff worry about losing their jobs, and that this fear needs to be addressed early.

talks.title: ZDC17: Panel Discussion - Strengthening The Cyber Resilience Of The Financial And Banking Sector
talks.teaser: ZDC17: Panel Discussion - Strengthening The Cyber Resilience Of The Financial And Banking Sector.
talks.summary:
### Overview
This panel discussion explores the state of cyber resilience, threat landscapes, and regulatory shifts within the banking and financial services sector. Moderated by Anton, the panel features industry leaders from banking, insurance, and enterprise technology: Richard Harper (FXO), Gary Delaney (AIB), Enda Devine (FBD), and Alan Jenkins (IBM). The conversation covers why financial institutions remain prime targets, how human behavior and legacy architectures impact defense postures, emerging compliance requirements like PSD2 and GDPR, and the vital necessity of inter-institution threat intelligence sharing.

### Key Topics
- **Attractiveness of Financial Institutions**: Criminals target banks directly because they can directly access and monetize funds rather than needing intermediate steps like selling stolen data or credit cards. The Bangladesh Central Bank cyber heist (via the SWIFT network) is highlighted as an example of a low-risk, high-return theft where $81 million was stolen, prevented from reaching $1 billion only by a spelling error.
- **Human Factor and Insider Risk**: End users and employees remain primary attack vectors. Phishing, social engineering, invoice redirection, and business email compromise (BEC) are common mechanisms where criminals manipulate employees into moving funds rather than breaching systems directly. Shadow IT and end-user computing (such as uncontrolled spreadsheets containing sensitive financial data) present major insider governance challenges.
- **Banking vs. Insurance Profiles**: Banks face direct transactional money extraction, whereas insurance companies traditionally deal with insurance fraud, ransomware, and sensitive data breaches. While insurers have historically operated on conservative, manual, face-to-face processes, legacy back-office systems (some older than 30 years) are increasingly being interfaced with modern digital customer-facing layers.
- **Fintech, APIs, and Regulation**: Innovations such as mobile banking, smart assistants (e.g., Alexa), Apple Pay, and regulatory mandates like PSD2 require banks to open APIs to third parties (e.g., accounting software). While driving customer convenience, these innovations introduce expanded attack surfaces and supply chain risks.
- **Board-Level Communication & Industry Collaboration**: Communicating cyber risk to executive boards requires framing security around business value, reputation protection, and solvency rather than technical jargon. The panel stresses that cybersecurity is non-competitive; institutions must collaborate, share threat intelligence, and satisfy formal regulatory expectations (such as guidance from the Central Bank of Ireland).

### Technical Details
- **Authentication and Network Controls**: Controls discussed include dedicated corporate devices, two-factor authentication (passwords and mobile devices), restricted C-drive access, strict email screening, and locked-down private networks.
- **Automated Containment and Response**: Techniques previously deployed in related high-risk environments include rapid endpoint containment (shutting down suspicious devices or servers within 5 to 10 minutes) and automated analysis tools like IBM Watson alongside 24/7 incident response operations.
- **End-User Computing Compliance**: Enforcing strict policies around sensitive data handling in spreadsheets to adhere to Sarbanes-Oxley (SOX) and GDPR governance through internal and external audit enforcement.

### Takeaways
Financial institutions operate under a mature fortress mentality, but legacy systems, rapid fintech disruption, and the human element remain significant vulnerabilities. Security leaders must bridge technical risk to board-level business metrics, maintain strong governance over end-user computing, and actively collaborate across the industry to protect the wider economic ecosystem.

talks.title: ZDC17: Panel Discussion - Ready, Set, Respond: Best Practice Cybersecurity Incident Plans
talks.teaser: Practitioners hear how organizations draft, test, and fund incident response plans when attacks force them to act alone.
talks.summary:
A moderated panel opens with survey data showing fewer organizations lack cyber incident response plans, while many still lack consistent deployment or repeat testing. Panelists from dairy processing, telecommunications security, enterprise technology marketing, and medical-device manufacturing compare how real incidents sharpened roles, trust during shift handovers, and ties to external communities such as regional IT forums.

Discussion covers connected manufacturing and legacy vendor software, minimum investments in tools versus skilled people, and framing security spend against business continuity rather than headline breaches alone. One panelist uses the Space Shuttle Challenger crisis room as an analogy for confirming facts, switching to contingency plans, and controlling who participates during stress. Others address GDPR-driven board attention, crisis exercises for executives, predictive analytics and AI in SIEM, and calibrating fear versus actionable threat focus without crying wolf.

Audience questions steer the close toward rapid threat change, five- to ten-minute response windows, strong partner information flows, training use cases, and whether culture change belongs in a fixed security budget or must come from leadership across the whole organization.

talks.title: ZDC17: Bryan McCarthy - Data Protection and the Law: The First Line of Defence... or the Last?
talks.teaser: ZDC17: Bryan McCarthy - Data Protection and the Law: The First Line of Defence... or the Last?.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk at Zero Day Con 2017, Bryan McCarthy, a data protection legal expert from Ronan Daly Jermyn, addresses the upcoming implementation of the European Union General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), which was roughly 14 months away from taking effect in May 2018. The presentation provides a practical legal analysis of the regulation's implications for organizations of all sizes, from tech startups to household consumer brands, focusing on shifting obligations, potential enforcement penalties, and the operational changes required to demonstrate compliance.

### Key Topics
- **Regulatory Fines and Scope**: Under GDPR's higher tier, administrative fines can reach up to €20 million or 4% of an organization's global annual turnover from the preceding financial year (whichever is greater), far exceeding the prior €100,000 maximum penalty under Irish data protection legislation. McCarthy illustrates this impact using Yahoo's 2013 breach (disclosed in 2016): with Yahoo's 2016 revenue north of $5.1 billion, equivalent penalties could have reached $240 million.
- **Extraterritorial Applicability**: GDPR applies regardless of where processing occurs if an organization sells goods or services to EU individuals or monitors the behavior of EU data subjects. Examples cited include an Australian firm marketing to Ireland, a phone accessories manufacturer in Shenzhen selling online to Irish consumers, or a San Francisco data analytics company monitoring Irish employees for performance evaluations.
- **Accountability and Privacy by Design**: Organizations must not only comply but actively demonstrate compliance. Mechanisms include adhering to guidance from the Data Protection Commissioner and European Data Protection Board, adopting accredited codes of conduct, certifications, and seals (valid up to three years), and implementing Privacy by Design—ensuring data privacy considerations are embedded at the initial conception of any business or operational change rather than treated as an afterthought at execution.

### Technical Details & Legal Mechanics
- **Consent Requirements**: Valid consent must be freely given, specific, informed, and unambiguous via clear affirmative action; pre-ticked boxes, silence, and inaction are prohibited. Subjects must have the right to withdraw consent as easily as it was given. For children, the default age threshold for valid consent is 16 (member states may lower it to no less than 13). Where consent is absent or invalid, controllers must identify another lawful basis, commonly legitimate interests, which requires balancing controller needs against data subject fundamental rights (applicable in areas like fraud prevention, intra-group transfers, and network or information security protection).
- **Data Protection Officers (DPOs)**: Mandatory for public authorities, entities conducting large-scale regular and systematic monitoring of individuals, or those processing sensitive personal data on a large scale. DPOs must have professional qualifications, report directly to top management, operate with genuine independence without receiving instructions, and cannot be dismissed for performing their duties.
- **Data Subject Rights & Access Requests**: Enhances rights such as erasure (right to be forgotten) and introduces data portability, allowing users to mandate the transfer of their data directly between providers. For standard Subject Access Requests (SARs), the response window is shortened from 40 days to 30 days (extendable by up to two additional months under specific conditions), and the former €6.35 statutory fee is abolished.
- **Breach Notification & Security Controls**: Controllers must implement appropriate technical and organizational measures evaluated against the state-of-the-art technological developments, cost of implementation, and nature of the processed data. In the event of a breach, supervisory authorities must be notified within 72 hours, and affected individuals must be informed without delay if the breach poses a high risk to their rights.

### Takeaways
McCarthy emphasizes that organizations have a strict 14-month countdown to evaluate existing data processing, review legacy consent mechanisms, evaluate international data transfer mechanisms (such as standard contractual clauses amid evolving case law), and align security practices with GDPR requirements before May 2018.

talks.title: ZDC17: Dave Allen - Tackling The Cyber Threat On The Journey To Cloud Security
talks.teaser: Walks through shifting cyber threats and shared-responsibility gaps that shape security decisions on the path to cloud adoption.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with threat history, starting with the 1989 AIDS Trojan, an early ransomware example that demanded payment. The speaker then shares threat intelligence gathered over about the last 90 days against Ireland, showing that finance and security sectors were heavily targeted, that web and email were the main vectors, and that Locky remained a prevalent ransomware family. Attackers, he argues, mostly want to steal data rather than only disrupt, and a 2007 denial-of-service attack on Estonia illustrates how political disputes can spill into cyber operations.

The middle section covers barriers to cloud adoption, with security and regulatory compliance named as the leading concerns. Responsibility has shifted as teams spin up services without involving IT, and the speaker separates private cloud, public cloud infrastructure and SaaS. Across these models, providers secure the underlying platform while customers remain accountable for their workloads, identities and data. He cites the 2014 Code Spaces incident, where an attacker took over its cloud environment and deleted its data, and points to the Cloud Security Alliance's list of top cloud threats.

The closing section presents a risk assessment approach built on classifying data, gaining visibility, blocking known threats with threat intelligence, and using analytics for unknown ones. Segmentation, including very short-lived virtual machines, is recommended, and the speaker argues that automated, integrated prevention across endpoints, data centers and cloud is the practical route.

talks.title: ZDC17: Tom Kellermann - Investing in Intrusion Suppression: Mitigating the Kill Chain of 2017
talks.teaser: Argues for intrusion suppression over perimeter models, combining deception grids, behavior analytics, and egress control to cut dwell time.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames modern breaches as sustained home invasions rather than burglaries, citing long adversary dwell times, wiper and destructive malware trends, and dark-web economies built around zero-day exploitation and remote access tooling. It walks through how intruders persist, move laterally, abuse supply chains, and monetize victims through secondary schemes such as business email compromise and watering hole abuse, including punitive retaliation when defenders detect them.

Tom Kellermann contrasts checklist frameworks and castle-style perimeters with an architectural metaphor drawn from high-security prison design: limiting situational awareness for anyone who gets inside. He introduces intrusion suppression as a defensive mantra that prioritizes stopping data and attackers from leaving the environment, not only blocking entry. Recommended capabilities include deception grids with full operating-system traps, user and entity behavior analytics, adaptive authentication, memory-augmented hunting, and deliberate choices about active response and attribution.

The talk closes by tying attack volume to geopolitics and naming expected trend lines—campaigns against influential targets, SaaS and mobile proximity abuse, denial of service as diversion, and lasting destructive attacks. Practitioners are urged to treat the problem as brand protection and to brief leadership accordingly.

talks.title: ZDC17: Denis Kennelly - Cognitive Security: A New Approach To Cyber Defence
talks.teaser: Explores how cognitive analytics connects SOC alerts with unstructured threat research for faster incident triage.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames today’s defensive challenge as an exploding attack surface and a flood of disconnected security products. Simple data-center controls gave way to online business, cloud, and billions of connected objects, while customers face roughly 1,500 vendors and a worsening skills gap. IBM Security’s response is described as an integrated, orchestrated platform—an “immune system” spanning endpoints, networks, identity, and partners—with federated data access rather than copying everything into one vendor silo, plus an open IBM App Exchange ecosystem.

The core of the talk is applying Watson-style cognitive processing to security operations. Analysts typically have limited time per alert and rely heavily on structured logs and threat feeds, while most relevant knowledge sits in unstructured blogs, papers, and social posts. The described system ingests feeds on short intervals, crawls on the order of a million security documents hourly, and exposes an on-site curator with an interface to ask whether an event is benign or part of something larger.

Customer examples include a South Carolina energy company where blocked malware tied to a broader campaign surfaced in minutes instead of nearly an hour without the tool, and a local beta deployment that linked a nearby ransomware effort. Reported benefits emphasize faster investigations, higher accuracy under time pressure, and consistent intelligence drawn from continually updated research.

talks.title: ZDC17: Martin Leahy - The Abtran Cybersecurity Journey
talks.teaser: A national-scale BPO outlines cloud-era risks, a live ransomware response, and lessons on data, monitoring, and workforce awareness.
talks.summary:
The talk positions Abtran, Ireland’s largest indigenous business-processing organization, between major clients and millions of customers, managing identity checks, calls, email, and utility payments. The speaker describes how engagements evolved from simple phone support and pin-style client links into a broad contact-center and analytics stack, then into a cloud-centered model where CRM, payments, and analytics run as software services while banks and utilities keep core systems on their side.

He argues that defenders must worry about behavior inside the company, cloud providers, and especially the patterns of traffic crossing those boundaries. Illustrations include everyday insider mishandling of data and industry-wide cooperation after an external researcher reported a serious flaw at a major traffic intermediary. The centerpiece is a ransomware-style incident on premises: ransom messaging, corruption on specific disk volumes, and no security monitoring until the attack accelerated an already planned project—after which centralized analysis showed the real aim was copying data out through the firewall, not merely disrupting storage.

The current posture combines next-generation firewalls, round-the-clock monitoring with an external partner, and AI-assisted analysis on the monitoring backend, with recent statistics on attack severities and blocked high-priority events. The closing recommendations are to staff and train a security function, inventory and classify data (and delete what lacks business purpose), educate a large agent workforce, and invest continuously in protection and monitoring while accepting that the core goals—preventing disclosure, theft, damage, or unauthorized change to data—remain the same.
